newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Lynyrd Skynyrd shows southern rock can rise again.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Lynyrd Skynyrd shows southern rock can rise again.

text.p: It's a musical comeback to rival the return of popular bands like the Eagles, the Sex Pistols and Kiss.

Almost 19 years after a plane crash killed several members of Lynyrd Skynyrd, the band's music is coming to movie theatres across the United States, and modern technology means the Southern rockers look and sound better than ever.
Although the group's signature songs such as "Sweet Home Alabama" crop up regularly on the radio and in film soundtracks, they have never appeared in a concert movie.
Until now. "Freebird -- The Movie," the result of eight years of painstaking research, is making its way through theatres in limited release.

For fans who never witnessed vocalist Ronnie Van Zant and the sizzling three-guitar attack, music critics say the film shows the seven-piece band from Jacksonville, Florida, justifying its reputation as one of the hottest live acts in the business.

Tragically, no one will ever know how far the band could have gone. On October 20, 1977, days after Lynyrd Skynyrd launched a tour to promote their newly released fifth studio album, their charter plane ran out of gas just short of a landing strip in McComb, Mississippi.
Van Zant, guitarist Steve Gaines, his back-up singer and sister Cassie Gaines, road manager Dean Kilpatrick and the two pilots died in the crash.

Guitarists Gary Rossington and Allen Collins (who died in 1990), bass player Leon Wilkeson and pianist Billy Powell went on to form the Rossington-Collins Band. They have since resurrected the Skynyrd name -- itself a tribute of sorts to Leonard Skinner, the high school gym teacher who suspended Rossington for having long hair -- and tour constantly.
"We kinda wanted to show the people where it all started from since it's still going on," Rossington, now 44, said in an interview.

The original incarnation lives on too, selling over a million albums a year, according to Van Zant's widow, Judy. Yet there has never been a Lynyrd Skynyrd movie, because of legal hurdles and the poor quality of the extant film footage.

"We're lucky to have what we have, and we're lucky that we did something with it when we did because of the condition (of the film)," she said in an interview. Van Zant worked with surviving band members as well as various estates and trusts to put the film together.

The movie concentrates on the band's English breakthrough at Knebworth in August 1976 where they reportedly upstaged the Rolling Stones. Old home movies and recent interviews add flavor to the proceedings. Fifteen songs, including "Saturday Night Special", "Working for MCA", and "Sweet Home Alabama" are delivered through the latest audio technology.
One hurdle that could have killed the project was getting permission to show "Free Bird," the 10-minute-plus song that ended the band's concerts and remains a staple of album rock radio.
The camera ran out at Knebworth, and she had to negotiate with the estate of rock promoter Bill Graham to use footage from the July 3, 1977 show at the Oakland Coliseum.

"They could have really taken us, since they have 'Free Bird'. We need 'Free Bird,' we can't really do it without that," she said. Her late husband's friendship with Graham helped save the day, although the clip itself tends to focus more on pretty girls in the audience than on the band.

Also featured is black and white footage from the July 13, 1977 show at Asbury Park, New Jersey where the band previewed the songs "What's Your Name" and "That Smell" from the eerily titled last album "Street Survivors." The film ends on a poignant note with 8mm home camera footage of the band relaxing on their plane just months before it went down.

But Van Zant wants the movie to be a fun experience. In addition to screening the film in theatres, she plans to show it in amphitheaters so that fans can drink beer and relax with their friends in a concert setting. A 13-song soundtrack has been released on MCA Records, and the home video will probably come out at the end of 1997.

Although she has remarried, Van Zant remains the driving force behind the original band. She is writing a book about Ronnie that she hopes to publish next year and which could be adapted for the big screen.

The band itself is finishing a tour and writing songs for a new album, Rossington says. "We're just doing a hard rock'n'roll album, coming back out and showing people what good rock'n'roll is, instead of country rock or southern rock. We're just a band from the south, we ain't southern musicians, we're just musicians. We're just going to carry on."
